brief_angle: When the algorithm flags an autistic candidate's low 'engagement' score for manual review, does the human reviewer overturn the machine's judgment or countersign it — is the flag functioning as a second chance or as a mark that primes the hand that touches it next?
notes: No other human actually speaks in this piece. The vendor's marketing copy is quoted, but the recruiter — your best material, the insider who complicates everything — only exists in summary and conditional mood: 'Her argument was that...', 'She would rather be measured by a number she can see.' You have her request in writing through the records office; get her actual words inside quotation marks, in the past tense, even one sentence from that HR filing. Right now the piece is a monologue in a sealed room, and she's the one voice that could break it open. Protect the blank-field ending though — her unresolved file is the payoff this piece earned.

Delete the sentences that announce your own moves before you make them: 'I want to tell you the obvious thing first, because it is true' (para 2), 'Here is what I did not expect' (para 8), 'I cannot make her disappear and I will not try' (end of para 8), and 'I have felt the pull of that position for years and I want to argue against it here, on its merits' (para 10). In every case the material underneath is strong — the spreadsheet reversal, the recruiter, the archive argument — and the announcement turns a turn the reader should feel into a requirement they watch being satisfied. Cut the signposts, keep everything under them.

You're several verdict-sentences over budget and they're cancelling each other out. 'That is the whole of it' (para 1), 'Nobody watched them. Nobody had to' (para 6), 'it depends, and the dependence is the scandal' (para 11), and 'it names a stranger who will decide whether resemblance is destiny' (para 11) are all doing the epigram thing within one draft. Keep one — I'd argue for the resemblance/destiny line since it completes the opening's claim — and flatten the others into plain prose. Also note the recruiter's implied line about published thresholds is sharper than most of yours; once she speaks in her own words, don't top her.
